title: Kindness, read again
hook: the loving-kindness discourse, read whole, start to finish
carry: as a mother her only child

segments.voice: Yesterday: the man who shouted outcast, and your line, what someone does, not where they're from. Did you treat someone as noble? Today, a text you've met before, read the whole way through. Day five hundred eighty-five.
screen: `WHAT SOMEONE DOES, NOT WHERE THEY'RE FROM.`

segments.voice: A radio edit trims a song down. Then one day the full album version plays, with the verse the radio left out, and the same song is suddenly bigger. More than a year ago, in the first months of this path, we spent days on loving-kindness, metta, and on its picture of a mother and her child. Now, reading the Sutta Nipata in order, we arrive at the poem itself, the eighth piece in the book. Ten short verses. Today we hear it start to finish, and notice the shape. Today's word: kindness.
screen: `THE ALBUM VERSION.` → `THE EIGHTH POEM IN THE BOOK.` → `START TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: The poem moves in three steps. First, how to live. Before any wishing, it describes a person: capable, upright, gentle, easy to speak to, not proud, content, not weighed down by busyness, calm in the senses, not greedy with families. Doing nothing the wise would criticize. Kindness starts as a way of behaving. Second, the wishes. May all beings be happy and at ease. Weak or strong, long or short, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born: may all beings be happy. Let no one deceive another or look down on anyone anywhere, or wish harm on anyone in anger. And then the image at the center: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Notice it's the boundlessness being compared: a love that doesn't measure. Third, the reach. Kindness spreading above, below and all around, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake, keep this mindfulness. This, the poem says, is called a divine way of living, right here. And the last verse turns. It doesn't end on love. It ends on seeing: not grasping at views, having clear vision, letting go of greed for sense pleasures, such a one won't be born again into a womb. Kindness, in this poem, isn't only warm. It's a path to waking up.
screen: `FIRST, HOW TO LIVE` · `THEN THE WISHES: ALL BEINGS` · `A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD` · `ABOVE, BELOW, ALL AROUND` · then, large: `AS A MOTHER HER ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite it, in your own way. Sit and settle. Say the wishes slowly, in the poem's order. May all beings be happy and at ease. The weak and the strong. The seen and the unseen. Those near and those far. Those born, and those yet to be born. Then picture the mother bent over her only child, and let that same unmeasured care spread out: above you, below you, all around. If you know the Pali, you can chant it instead. Then rest inside that wide feeling. The bell holds the time.
Kindness. Metta, as the poem lays it out whole: a way of living, a set of wishes for all beings, and a boundless heart spreading in every direction. Today's word.
Your line: as a mother her only child. Today, when you're standing, walking or sitting somewhere ordinary, send the poem's wish to everyone in sight. Day five hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: The Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted in Pali in Theravada temples and homes, often from memory, as one of the protective chants called paritta.

fork.setup: you're reading the kindness poem for the first time. it's about to describe the heart it asks for toward all beings. what picture does it use?
options: a mother protecting her only child with her life.
fork.reveal: a mother and her only child: the comparison is to love without measure, spread to every being.

original.note: Pali metta (Sanskrit maitri): loving-kindness, friendliness, from mitta, friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: the metta sutta is a sweet poem about feeling love for everyone.
what it means: it moves from conduct, to wishes for all beings, to kindness filling every direction, and ends on clear seeing.

what a scholar hears: the mother verse can be read as comparing the boundlessness of the heart rather than literal protection; the poem appears in both the Sutta Nipata (1.8) and the Khuddakapatha (9).

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (also Khuddakapatha 9)

notes: Sn 1.8 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the order and wording of the qualities, the wishes, the mother verse, the 'above, below, across' verse, the four postures and 'brahma-viharam idam ahu', and the closing verse.
Day 105 covered this sutta and the commentary story of the forest monks; this day takes the whole-poem, three-movement angle.
The reading that the mother verse compares boundlessness is one interpretation (the grammar of anurakkhe and the comparison is discussed by translators); presented as one reading.
'Ten short verses' is the usual count in the Pali; confirm.
